title: Order: a timer, a promise, synchronous code
prompt: The classic opening question about the event loop.
explanation: The synchronous code runs to completion: `start`, `end`. Then the engine drains the microtask queue — the `then` callback is there, hence `promise`. The `setTimeout` macrotask gets its turn last, even with a zero delay.

title: Microtasks inside a macrotask
prompt: What matters here is that the microtask queue is drained **between** macrotasks.
explanation: The microtask `p0` goes first. Then the first macrotask prints `t1` and queues a microtask. Before moving on to the second macrotask the engine must drain the microtask queue — which is why `p1` comes before `t2`.

title: async/await and the order of execution
prompt: `await` cuts the function in two: everything after it becomes a microtask.
explanation: The body of an `async` function up to the first `await` runs synchronously — hence `1`. Then the function is suspended, control returns to the caller and `3` is printed. The continuation after `await null` was queued as a microtask before the `then`, so `2` comes before `4`.

title: this in a method and in an arrow
prompt: An arrow function has no `this` of its own.
explanation: `obj.regular()` is called as a method — `this` is `obj`. Inside `scoped` the arrow takes `this` from the surrounding method and also sees `obj`, while the plain function is called with no receiver: in strict mode its `this` is `undefined`. The detached `detached()` loses its receiver for the same reason.

title: A closure in a loop
prompt: The difference between `var` and `let` in a single line.
explanation: `var i` is a single variable for the whole function scope: all three callbacks closed over it, and by the time they run the loop has pushed `i` to 3. `let j` creates a fresh binding on every iteration, so each callback sees its own value.

title: Hoisting of declarations
prompt: What is hoisted whole and what is hoisted by name only.
explanation: A function declaration is hoisted whole, so `typeof fn` is already `function`. `var value` is hoisted without its value — `undefined`. `let later` is hoisted too, but it sits in the temporal dead zone: touching it before the declaration throws a `ReferenceError`.

title: Type coercion in comparisons
prompt: Every line is a separate `==` trap.
explanation: `[]` is coerced to an empty string, which becomes `0`, and `false` becomes `0` as well. `![]` is `false`, and from there it is the same story. `'0'` is coerced to the number `0`. `null == undefined` is a special rule of the language; with any other value, `0` included, `null` equals nothing. `NaN` equals nothing, itself included.

title: Promise.all versus allSettled
prompt: What happens to the other promises when one of them fails.
explanation:
`Promise.all` rejects on the very first error — the other promises are not cancelled, their results are simply of no use to anyone. `allSettled` waits for all of them and never rejects: it hands back a list of objects with a `status` and a `value`/`reason`.

The order of the output here is not obvious: `allSettled` gets there first because both chains consist of microtasks, and `all` has one extra step before it reaches `catch`.

title: What flows down a then chain
prompt: The value returned by each handler becomes the input of the next one.
code:
Promise.resolve(1)
  .then((v) => { console.log('a', v); })
  .then((v) => { console.log('b', v); return 2; })
  .then((v) => { console.log('c', v); throw new Error('x'); })
  .catch((e) => { console.log('d', e.message); return 3; })
  .finally(() => { console.log('e'); return 99; })
  .then((v) => console.log('f', v));
explanation: A handler without a `return` yields `undefined` — hence `b undefined`. A thrown error takes the chain to the nearest `catch`, which swallows it and returns `3`. `finally` receives the outcome as is and ignores its own return value — so `f` gets `3`, not `99`.

title: sort without a comparator
prompt: Why numbers do not sort the way you expect.
explanation: Without a comparator `sort` converts the elements to strings: `'10' < '9'` lexicographically. With the comparator `a - b` you get numeric order. The third line is a reminder that `sort` mutates the original array and returns that very array — the reference is the same.

title: Shallow copying
prompt: What exactly does spread copy.
explanation: Spread copies only the top level: `a` became independent, while `nested` stayed a shared reference — a change through the copy is visible in the original. For an independent copy you need `structuredClone`.

title: The order of an object's keys
prompt: Integer-like keys behave differently from the rest.
explanation: In an object the integer-like keys come first in ascending order, and the other string keys follow in insertion order. An object's keys are always strings, so `2` became `'2'`. A `Map` preserves both the insertion order and the types of the keys.

title: reduce without an initial value
prompt: The initial value is not a formality.
explanation: Without an initial value the first element becomes the first accumulator and the iteration starts from the second one. On an empty array there is nothing to take — `reduce` throws a `TypeError`.

title: A default value in destructuring
prompt: The default does not fire for every kind of “emptiness”.
explanation: A default value is substituted strictly for `undefined`. `null`, `0` and an empty string pass through as they are — the same distinction as between `||` and `??`.

title: The values of a generator
prompt: `next(value)` can pass a value back in.
explanation: The first `next()` runs to the first `yield` and hands back `1`; the argument of that call is lost — there is nobody to receive it. `next(10)` supplies `10` as the result of the `yield 1` expression. After the `return` the generator is finished, and further calls give `undefined` with `done: true`.

title: The order class fields are initialised in
prompt: The base constructor runs before the subclass's fields.
explanation: The method is resolved dynamically, so the subclass's overridden `describe` is called. But the subclass's fields are initialised **after** `super()` returns, and at the moment of the call `label` has not been assigned yet. This is one of the most common traps of inheritance.

title: Independent closures
prompt: Every call to the factory creates its own environment.
explanation: Each call to `makeCounter` creates a new `count` variable and a new closure, so the counters are independent. From outside, `count` is unreachable — `typeof` is the one operator that does not throw a `ReferenceError` on an undeclared variable and returns `'undefined'` instead.

title: return inside finally
prompt: `finally` is able to override the result.
explanation: `finally` always runs, but it substitutes its own value only when it contains an explicit `return`. In `g` the value returned from `try` is lost — and this is a reliable way to swallow an exception by accident too, which is why a `return` inside `finally` is considered an anti-pattern.

title: try/catch and asynchrony
prompt: Why the wrapper does not catch the callback's error.
expectedOutput: caught inside the callback: from the timer
explanation: The outer `catch` never fires: `setTimeout` merely queues the callback and returns, and by the time it runs the stack holding the `try` has been unwound. The error can only be caught inside the callback itself — or, if it is not caught, it goes to the global handler without disturbing the surrounding code.

title: Set, NaN and objects
prompt: A Set compares by SameValueZero.
explanation: The numeric `1` and the string `'1'` are different values, and the duplicate `1` was dropped. Two `NaN`s count as the same value (SameValueZero), so `has(NaN)` is true. Two empty object literals are different references, and the third `{}` inside `has` is a new reference as well.

title: Getters and spread
prompt: Spread evaluates getters.
explanation: Spread copies the **result** of the getter rather than the getter itself: it is called exactly once, and the copy is left with an ordinary property holding a value. To preserve the accessor you need `Object.defineProperties` with `Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptors`.

title: Sparse arrays
prompt: Holes in an array do not behave like `undefined`.
explanation: A skipped element is not an `undefined` but a missing index. `map` preserves the hole and does not call the callback for it (which is why the output has a gap there), `in` returns `false`, and `Object.keys` skips the index. This is exactly why `Array(3).map(...)` fills nothing — you need `Array.from({ length: 3 })`.

title: The reverse mapping of an enum
prompt: A numeric `enum` produces a runtime object with two kinds of keys.
explanation: A numeric enum compiles into an object holding both a forward and a reverse mapping — hence four keys instead of two. A string enum has no reverse mapping. This is one of the reasons people often take a union of literals with `as const` instead of an `enum`.

title: Parameter properties and field initialisation
prompt: The shorthand `constructor(private label)` assigns the field somewhere other than where it looks.

title: as const and satisfies at runtime
prompt: A check that type-level constructs add nothing to the output.
explanation: `as const` is a type-level construct: it makes the fields `readonly` for the compiler but never calls `Object.freeze`, so the object is not frozen. `satisfies` verifies conformance to a type and disappears entirely at compile time. Neither of them emits any code.

title: Type erasure
prompt: Generics exist at compile time only.
explanation: After compilation nothing is left of `T`: inspecting a type parameter at runtime is impossible, and `box.constructor.name` gives plain `Box`. Hence `firstOf<string>([])` returning `undefined` despite the `T | undefined` signature — the compiler knows nothing about the array being empty.

title: Optional chaining and ??
prompt: Zero and an empty string are valid values.
explanation: `||` substitutes the fallback for any falsy value, so an empty string and a zero are lost. `??` reacts only to `null` and `undefined`. Optional chaining on a missing `address` yields `undefined` without throwing.

title: private in TypeScript and a #field
prompt: One restriction exists only for the compiler, the other one for real.
explanation: `private` in TypeScript is a compile-time agreement: at runtime it is an ordinary enumerable property, reachable through a cast to `any` and included in `JSON.stringify`. A `#` field is a genuine private field of the language: it appears neither in `Object.keys` nor in the serialisation.
